claims.text: Lau's CS 341 Lecture 5 lists 'To determine whether a given graph is connected' among the basic graph questions and says breadth-first search answers it in O(n + m) time (n vertices, m edges; the same slide deck says this running time is for adjacency lists).

support.locator: page 4, slide after the connectivity definitions
support.quote: To determine whether a given graph is connected.
Breadth first search (BFS) can be used to answer all these questions in 𝑂(𝑛 + 𝑚) time.
We will mostly use adjacency list, as this allows us to design 𝑂(𝑛 + 𝑚)-time algorithm.

claims.text: Lau's slides state the BFS correctness lemma from a start vertex s: there is a path from s to v if and only if v is marked visited when the search ends. The word 'path' is not defined for the lemma on the slides read; its proof is on image-only slides and was not read.

support.quote: Lemma. There is a path from 𝑠 to 𝑣 if and only if 𝑣𝑖𝑠𝑖𝑡𝑒𝑑 𝑣 = 𝑡𝑟𝑢𝑒 at the end.

claims.text: McCauley's Lecture 4 states that in a connected undirected graph BFS from any vertex s visits every vertex, and that if the graph is not connected BFS will not visit all nodes.

support.quote: In any connected undirected graph G, BFS starting at vertex s will visit every vertex.

support.locator: page 7, after the example graph with two triangles
support.quote: If the graph is not connected, BFS will not visit all nodes.

claims.text: Breadth-first search from n_1 is a second test of connectivity: G is connected exactly when the search from n_1 visits all N vertices. This restates m3-2 and m3-3 for the start vertex n_1 and the paper's definition of connected; the sources do not state it in exactly this form. The paper does not prove the BFS lemma; it is cited.

support.quote: Lemma. There is a path from 𝑠 to 𝑣 if and only if 𝑣𝑖𝑠𝑖𝑡𝑒𝑑 𝑣 = 𝑡𝑟𝑢𝑒 at the end.
In any connected undirected graph G, BFS starting at vertex s will visit every vertex.

claims.text: Reachability lemma (derived): for vertices n_i and n_j with i not equal to j, a path (no repeated vertex) from n_i to n_j exists if and only if (A^k)_ij > 0 for some k with 1 <= k <= N - 1. Proof: a path of length k has k + 1 distinct vertices so 1 <= k <= N - 1, and is a walk, so the walk-counting theorem gives (A^k)_ij >= 1; conversely a positive entry is a walk of length k, which contains a path of length at most k <= N - 1.

support.locator: Theorem 1.1.3, printed p. 4 (premise: walk counting, module m1)
support.quote: Then the entry in the (i, j)-position of the matrix Ak is the number of walks of length k from vi to vj in G.

support.locator: Corollary 2.9.7, p. 39 (premise: walk contains a path, module m2)
support.quote: Assume that there is a walk from u to v of length k for some k ∈ N. Then, there is a path from u to v of length ≤ k.

support.locator: Section 2.9.4, p. 40 (premise: path length at most N - 1)
support.quote: any path from u to v must have length ≤ n − 1, where n is the number of vertices of G

claims.text: Sum test (derived): G is connected if and only if every off-diagonal entry of B = A + A^2 + ... + A^(N-1) is positive. The entries of each A^k are non-negative integers, so B_ij > 0 exactly when some (A^k)_ij > 0 with 1 <= k <= N - 1, and Lemma M3.1 finishes. The statement is Paramadevan and Sotheeswaran Theorem 2; the proof here goes through the walk-to-path lemma that their proof omits (C43).

support.quote: Then, AG is connected if and only if bij ≠ 0, when i ≠ j.

claims.text: Power test (derived): G is connected if and only if (I + A)^(N-1) has no zero entry. Because I and A commute, (I + A)^(N-1) = sum over k = 0 to N-1 of C(N-1, k) A^k with every coefficient at least 1; off the diagonal this is positive exactly when B_ij > 0, and the k = 0 term makes every diagonal entry at least 1. The statement is Gotti Proposition 3 and Bai Theorem 2; the equivalence with the sum test is shown here (C52).

support.quote: Then G is connected if and only if all the entries of (In + A)n−1 are positive.
Then G is connected if and only if the matrix power (I + A)n−1 has all entries strictly positive.

claims.text: The relation alpha (u alpha v if there is a path from u to v, length 0 allowed) is reflexive, symmetric and transitive (derived: reverse a walk; join two walks and cut the result to a path with the walk-to-path lemma). The textbook only notes this on printed p. 49, without proof; the proof is the paper's own. Components are the induced subgraphs on the classes, and the graph is connected exactly when there is one class (the textbook's Remark 2.1.1).

support.locator: printed p. 49, prose after Definition 2.1.1 (viewed as image)

claims.text: The textbook's Definition 2.1.1 uses the book's 'path' (a walk with no repeated edge, English trail), the course convention uses the vertex-distinct path. The two give the same notion of connected (derived): a vertex-distinct path of length at least 1 has no repeated edge, so it is a trail; a trail is a walk, which contains a vertex-distinct path with the same ends.

claims.text: Worked examples (computed): for the board matrix (edges n1n2 and n2n3), A^2 = [[1,0,1],[0,2,0],[1,0,1]], B = A + A^2 = [[1,1,1],[1,2,1],[1,1,1]], (I + A)^2 = [[2,2,1],[2,3,2],[1,2,2]]: no zero entry, connected. For the disconnected graph (edge n1n2, n3 isolated), A^2 = [[1,0,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,0]], B = [[1,1,0],[1,1,0],[0,0,0]], (I + A)^2 = [[2,2,0],[2,2,0],[0,0,1]]: B_13 = B_23 = B_31 = B_32 = 0, not connected. Second connected example: triangle, B and (I + A)^2 all positive.
claims.derivation: scripts/m3_connectivity.py, output recorded in modules/m3.md Section 5

claims.text: A single power is not a test and the diagonal must be ignored (computed): on the path n1, n2, n3, (A^2)_12 = 0 although n1n2 is an edge, because walks from n1 to n2 have odd length; for N = 2 with one edge, B = A has a zero diagonal while the graph is connected; in the disconnected example (A^2)_33 = 0 for the isolated vertex.

Computational check, not a proof: on every labelled simple graph with N = 1 to 6 vertices (1, 2, 8, 64, 1024, 32768 graphs; 1, 1, 4, 38, 728, 26704 of them connected) the sum test, the (I + A)^(N-1) test and an independent breadth-first search agree on all graphs, with zero disagreements.
claims.derivation: scripts/m3_connectivity.py, last block of its output, recorded in modules/m3.md Section 5

claims.text: Cost remark (estimate from counting, not a measurement): computing B or (I + A)^(N-1) from the definition of the matrix product takes N - 2 products of N by N matrices, each product N^3 multiplications; BFS on an adjacency matrix scans one row of N entries per visited vertex, so about N^2 steps; with adjacency lists the slides give O(n + m).

support.quote: Breadth first search (BFS) can be used to answer all these questions in 𝑂(𝑛 + 𝑚) time.
